findings.claim: Every lesson labels its practice questions “15 marks — Extract Response” or “25 marks — Essay Response”, with band ladders keyed to 13-15/21-25. Lesson 1's exam tip says context (AO3) is “worth 25 marks in part (b)”; lesson 2's says part (a) is “15 marks, AO2”; lesson 5's says part (b) is “25 marks, AO1 + AO3”; lesson 7's tip says spend 15 minutes on part (a) and 25 on part (b); lesson 7's first knowledge check keys “15 marks” as the value of part (a).
findings.truth: The Edexcel Shakespeare question is two parts of 20 marks each. Part (a) is 20 marks, AO2 only. Part (b) is 20 marks, AO1 15 + AO3 5, with no SPaG credit (AO4 is 8 marks and sits only on the post-1914 essay). The paper is 80 marks in 1 hour 45 minutes, closed book, so Section A deserves about 25 minutes per part. The 15 + 25 split belongs to a different board.
findings.evidence: specs/edexcel/english-literature-1ET0.md lines 1102-1113 (part a AO2, part b AO1+AO3, closed book, 80 marks, 1h45) and the raw mark distribution table at lines 1312-1350: questions 1a-6a = AO2 20, total 20; questions 1b-6b = AO1 15 + AO3 5, total 20; questions 7-30 = AO1 16 + AO3 16 + AO4 8, total 40

findings.truth: “Component 1” is a banned string; the house validator rejects the whole unit. Rewritten as “the Edexcel Shakespeare question” in the same edit that corrects the marks.

findings.claim: “Don John tells Claudio that Don Pedro is wooing Hero for himself: ‘the Prince woos for himself.’”
findings.truth: Don John does mislead Claudio (“my brother is amorous on Hero”), but the quoted words are Claudio's own, spoken alone on stage after Don John and Borachio leave. A student who attributes the line to Don John misquotes the speaker.
findings.evidence: much-ado.txt line 1082, Act 2 Scene 1: CLAUDIO. ‘Tis certain so; the Prince woos for himself. Don John's speech is at lines 1046-1049.

findings.claim: In the gulling of Benedick the conspirators say Beatrice is “so beyond all measure” in her affection.
findings.truth: Fabricated quotation. The phrase does not appear in the play. Leonato's actual words are “she loves him with an enraged affection: it is past the infinite of thought”. The second half of the sentence (“falls, weeps, sobs…”) is genuine and is Claudio's.
findings.evidence: much-ado.txt lines 1625-1627 (Leonato) and line 1703 (Claudio), Act 2 Scene 3; no match anywhere for ‘beyond all measure’

findings.claim: “The Friar… observes what no one else will: ‘Is it not Hero? Who can blot that name / With any just reproach?’”
findings.truth: Hero speaks those two lines herself, answering Claudio's catechising. The Friar's own defence of her comes later and rests on reading her blushes.
findings.evidence: much-ado.txt lines 3012-3013, Act 4 Scene 1: HERO. Is it not Hero? Who can blot that name / With any just reproach?

findings.claim: Dogberry's malapropisms include calling himself “an ass” and declaring suspects should be “condemnified”.
findings.truth: “Condemnified” is not in the play — a fabricated quotation. Dogberry's real blunder there is “condemned into everlasting redemption” (he means damnation). “An ass” is not a malapropism either: he is repeating, in indignation, the insult Conrade threw at him and demanding it be written down. “Aspicious” for “suspicious” is correct and is kept.
findings.evidence: much-ado.txt line 3532 (‘condemned into everlasting redemption’, 4.2), line 3577 (‘O that I had been writ down an ass!’), line 4013 (‘that I am an ass’, 5.1), line 2814 (‘aspicious’, 3.5), line 3432 (‘dissembly’, 4.2); no match for ‘condemnified’

findings.claim: “excellent material for a Level 5 AO1 response”
findings.truth: Banned band name. Replaced with “top-band” from the house ladder.

findings.claim: “When the evidence of their tricked love letters is produced, he says: ‘Thou and I are too wise to woo peaceably’.”
findings.truth: That line is spoken in Act 5 Scene 2, alone with Beatrice in the garden, well before the letters surface. The letters are produced in Act 5 Scene 4, where Benedick says “I take thee for pity” and then “Peace! I will stop your mouth”. The lesson's own practice question labels the line 5.2 correctly, so the prose contradicts it.

findings.claim: “His malapropisms (‘Write down that they are none’ when he means ‘note’)”
findings.truth: Not a malapropism, and the gloss is meaningless. The real line is “Have you writ down, that they are none?” — Dogberry solemnly minuting the prisoners' denial as though it were evidence. No word is confused with a similar-sounding one. Replaced with two genuine malapropisms.

findings.claim: “Dogberry's malapropisms — ‘Are you good men and true?’”, and the flashcard “Which Dogberry malapropism accidentally frames the play's truth question?”
findings.truth: “Are you good men and true?” is plain, correct English and contains no malapropism. A student naming it as one in an AO2 answer would be wrong. The line's thematic point stands; only the label is wrong.

findings.claim: “Starting with Act 1, Scene 1, explain how Shakespeare presents… Write about this extract and the play as a whole.”
findings.truth: That is another board's fixed question formula. Edexcel part (b) asks how a theme reflected in the printed extract is explored elsewhere in the play. Stem rewritten to the Edexcel shape.

findings.claim: “Which Beatrice line expresses her rejection of marriage through a canine simile?”
findings.truth: “I had rather hear my dog bark at a crow than a man swear he loves me” is a comparative preference, not a simile — there is no ‘like’ or ‘as’ construction. Naming the wrong device costs AO2 credit.

findings.claim: The matching question labels a deception “Window scene (3.3)”.
findings.truth: Shakespeare never stages the window scene. Borachio plans it in Act 2 Scene 2 and boasts about it to Conrade in Act 3 Scene 3, where the Watch overhear him; the deception itself happens offstage. The pairing is right, only the scene label is wrong.
findings.evidence: much-ado.txt Act 2 Scene 2 (lines 1383-1460) and Act 3 Scene 3 (lines 2282-2563)

findings.claim: “I pray you, is Signor Mountanto returned from the wars?”
findings.truth: The line reads “Signior Mountanto returned from the wars or no?” The spelling and the trimmed tail are not mark-affecting in a closed-book exam, and the spelling recurs in a knowledge check and a flashcard, so an edit would ripple for no gain.

findings.claim: “Most GCSE Shakespeare questions combine two tasks… Check your exam board's specimen paper for the exact format… Many boards run this as a closed book exam.”
findings.truth: Nothing here is false, but a board-specific unit should not hedge. The Edexcel paper definitely is closed book and definitely is a two-part question. The hedging is what let the wrong 15/25 marks survive elsewhere in the unit. Worth tightening on the next content pass, not by a fact-check edit.

findings.claim: “Benedick switches to verse in Act 5, Scene 2 when he tries to write a love poem for Beatrice and fails miserably… The switch from prose to clumsy verse is comic.”
findings.truth: Two defensible readings. He does sing a snatch of verse at the start of 5.2 (“The god of love, / That sits above”) and says he has tried to write a sonnet, which supports ‘switches to verse’. But the quoted line is his prose admission that he cannot find a rhyme, so the joke is arguably that he never manages verse at all. Either keep the claim and cite the sung snatch as the evidence, or soften ‘switches to verse’ to ‘reaches for verse’. Not edited.

summary: No lesson is clean: all seven carry the board-format fault, because every practice question, three exam tips, the timing advice and one knowledge-check key are built on a 15 + 25 mark split that belongs to another board, where Edexcel sets two 20-mark parts (part a AO2, part b AO1 15 + AO3 5, no SPaG). On top of that there are three misattributed or fabricated quotations (‘the Prince woos for himself’ is Claudio's, ‘Is it not Hero? Who can blot that name’ is Hero's, and ‘so beyond all measure’ and ‘condemnified’ are not in the play) and three things wrongly labelled malapropisms. None of the four faults found in the AQA Much Ado unit recur here.
